analogy.p: Imagine a delivery lorry dropping parcels at a town. A tiny village has a short high street, so every house is only a few steps from the road and everyone gets their parcel at once. A huge city has the same kind of road on its outside edge, but millions of houses are far from it. The city only works because it has a network of inner streets and delivery vans (a transport system) and big depots (exchange surfaces). The analogy breaks down because a city's inner roads are built by planners, whereas cells receive substances passively by diffusion and need no 'driver'.

bullets: Cells need **oxygen** and **dissolved food (glucose, amino acids)** coming in, and must remove **carbon dioxide** and **urea (waste)**.

**Diffusion** is the spreading out of particles from a region of **higher concentration** to a region of **lower concentration** (down a concentration gradient). It is a **passive** process, so it needs **no energy** from the cell.
The substances that cross cell membranes by diffusion include **oxygen, carbon dioxide, urea and dissolved small molecules** (the particles must be small enough to pass through the membrane).
The **rate** of diffusion is affected by three factors in the spec: the **concentration difference (gradient)**, the **temperature**, and the **surface area of the membrane**.
Link: this is the same idea you use later for **gas exchange in the lungs, absorption in the small intestine, gills in fish and roots/leaves in plants**.
core.h: Why exchange matters: the needs of every cell
core.p: Every living cell must take in the substances it needs and get rid of waste. Oxygen and glucose are needed for **aerobic respiration**, which releases the energy for life processes, while **carbon dioxide and urea** are waste products that must leave. In small organisms these substances simply **diffuse** across the outer surface. The bigger an organism gets, the harder this becomes, and that is why SA:V is such an important idea in biology.

bullets: **Surface area** is measured in square units (**cm²**, **m²**); **volume** is measured in cubic units (**cm³**, **m³**).
The **SA:V ratio** = **surface area ÷ volume**. It is usually written as **'X : 1'** by dividing both sides by the volume.
The **surface** is where exchange happens, but the **volume** is what needs supplying (the amount of cytoplasm using oxygen and making waste).
A **high** SA:V means a lot of surface for exchange compared with the amount of cell that needs supplying; a **low** SA:V means the opposite.
The ratio has **no units** when written as a simple ratio (although the area and volume have units before you divide).
core.h: What surface area and volume mean
core.p: **Surface area** is the total area of the outside of an object, which is the area through which substances can enter or leave. **Volume** is the amount of space inside, which is a measure of how much living material there is that needs supplying. So the **surface area to volume ratio** compares how much 'doorway' an organism has with how much 'house' it must serve. A large SA:V means plenty of surface for each bit of volume, so exchange is easy.

bullets: **Step 1:** find the area of one face (L × L). **Step 2:** multiply by 6 for the surface area. **Step 3:** find the volume (L × L × L). **Step 4:** divide the surface area by the volume.
**1 cm cube:** SA = 6 × 1² = 6 cm²; V = 1 cm³; **SA:V = 6 : 1**.
**4 cm cube:** SA = 96 cm²; V = 64 cm³; SA:V = **1.5 : 1**. **6 cm cube:** SA = 216 cm²; V = 216 cm³; SA:V = **1 : 1**.
For a **cuboid** (length l, width w, height h): **SA = 2(lw + lh + wh)** and **V = lwh**. Always add **all six faces**.
If the ratio does not come out whole, give it to **1 or 2 decimal places** (for example 2.17 : 1 is 2.2 : 1 to 1 d.p.).
core.h: How to calculate SA:V for cubes (step by step)
core.p: For a cube of side length L, each face is a square of area L × L, and there are **6 faces**, so the surface area is **6 × L²**. The volume is **L × L × L = L³**. Dividing, SA:V = 6L² ÷ L³ = **6 ÷ L**. You can use this shortcut to check your working, but in an exam you should still show surface area and volume separately because the marks are for each step.

bullets: Doubling the side: SA × 4, V × 8, so SA:V is **halved** (6:1 → 3:1).
Tripling the side: SA × 9, V × 27, so SA:V is **one third** (6:1 → 2:1).
A graph of SA:V against side length is a **curve that falls steeply then levels off** (it is SA:V = 6 ÷ side, an inverse relationship).
**Small objects have a large SA:V; large objects have a small SA:V.** This is true for cubes, cells and whole animals.
The same idea applies to **different shapes**: a flat, thin or folded shape has a bigger SA:V than a ball of the same volume (a sphere has the **smallest** SA:V for its volume).
In an exam you must be able to **state the pattern and give the reason**: 'volume increases faster than surface area'.
core.h: The pattern: bigger objects have a smaller SA:V
core.p: When a cube's side doubles, its surface area increases by a factor of **4** (2²), but its volume increases by a factor of **8** (2³). Volume grows faster than surface area, so the ratio gets smaller. This is a general rule for any shape: as an object gets bigger, **volume increases faster than surface area**, so SA:V **decreases**. It is the single most important conclusion of this topic.

bullets: The spec statement: a single-celled organism has a **relatively large surface area to volume ratio**, which **allows sufficient transport of molecules into and out of the cell to meet the needs of the organism**.
The distance from the membrane to the centre of the cell is tiny, so **diffusion is fast enough**.
Such organisms do not need specialised exchange organs or a circulatory system.
Examples: **amoeba, bacteria, yeast, Chlamydomonas** (a single-celled alga). Exchange happens across the **whole cell membrane** (and cell wall where present).
Even in single cells, shapes like **long thin or folded** cells increase SA:V further (for example root hair cells in plants, microvilli on intestinal cells).
core.p: A single-celled organism such as an amoeba or a bacterium is tiny, so it has a **relatively large surface area to volume ratio**. Every part of its cytoplasm is very close to the cell membrane, so the **diffusion distance is short**. Because of this, diffusion across the cell surface supplies enough oxygen and food and removes enough waste to meet the organism's needs. It needs no lungs, gills or blood.

bullets: The spec statement: **multicellular organisms have a smaller surface area to volume ratio** and the **diffusion distance is greater**, so they cannot meet their needs by diffusion across the outer surface alone.
Many cells are **deep inside** the body, so substances would take far too long to diffuse in from outside.
Larger organisms also have a **greater demand** because they have more cells respiring.
Solution 1: **exchange surfaces** (for example lungs, small intestine, gills, root hairs) to give a large area where substances cross.
Solution 2: a **transport system** (blood in animals, xylem and phloem in plants) to carry substances between the exchange surface and all the body cells.
Link: this links to **multicellular organisation** (cells → tissues → organs → organ systems) and to **why organisms need circulatory systems**.
core.h: Multicellular organisms: small SA:V and the problem it creates
core.p: In a large multicellular organism such as a human, the surface area of the skin is small compared with the enormous volume of the body. Most cells are deep inside and are **far from the outside**, so diffusion across the body surface would be far too slow to supply them. The organism's **SA:V is small**, so it cannot rely on its outer surface. Instead, multicellular organisms evolved specialised **exchange surfaces** and **transport systems** that carry substances to and from every cell.

bullets: **Large surface area**: provides more space for particles to cross at once. Achieved by **folding, villi, alveoli, many small branches**.
**Thin membrane / short diffusion path**: the distance particles must travel is small, so diffusion is quicker (often a membrane only **one cell thick**).
**Efficient blood supply** (animals): the blood **removes** diffusing substances as soon as they cross (or brings them), maintaining a **steep concentration gradient**.
**Ventilation** (for gas exchange in animals): moving air in and out keeps the concentration gradient steep.
In **plants**, leaves are thin and flat with many air spaces and stomata, and root hair cells have a large surface area for water and mineral uptake.
**Remember the logic:** each adaptation either increases surface area, shortens the path, or keeps the concentration gradient steep, which all **increase the rate of diffusion**.
core.h: Features that make an effective exchange surface
core.p: Exchange surfaces are specialised areas designed to make diffusion happen as quickly as possible. They work by following the factors that increase the rate of diffusion. You must be able to explain how a particular surface is adapted by linking each feature to its effect (large area, short path, steep gradient). Examiners expect you to name the feature AND give its function.

bullets: **Alveoli (lungs):** millions of tiny air sacs give a huge surface area; walls are **one cell thick**; surrounded by **capillaries** giving a good blood supply; breathing ventilates them.
**Villi (small intestine):** folds on the lining increase surface area; thin wall; rich blood supply carries absorbed food away, keeping the gradient steep.
**Gills (fish):** many thin filaments covered in lamellae give a large area; blood flow and water flow maintain the gradient.
**Root hair cells (plants):** long thin extensions increase the surface area for absorbing water by osmosis and mineral ions by active transport.
**Leaves:** flat and thin, with air spaces inside the spongy mesophyll to give a large internal surface for gas exchange.
Link: for each of these you should also be able to link the structure to its **function** in extended-response answers.
core.p: You should be able to apply the three ideas to examples met elsewhere in the course. Learning these now means you can write confident answers about adaptations in unfamiliar contexts. The principle is always the same: large area, thin, good gradient.

bullets: **Method:** cut agar cubes of different sizes (for example 1 cm, 2 cm, 3 cm); place each in acid; time how long until the pink disappears (or measure the depth of colour change after a fixed time).

**Independent variable:** cube size (and so SA:V). **Dependent variable:** time to go colourless (or distance diffused). **Control variables:** acid concentration and volume, temperature, same agar mixture.
**Result:** the **smaller cube** (higher SA:V) turns colourless **faster**; the acid reaches the centre quickly.
**Explanation:** the acid diffuses the same distance in the same time, but in a larger cube there is more volume further from the surface, so it takes **longer to reach the centre**.
**Why agar?** It is a good model of a cell because it is clear, a gel, and lets substances diffuse in.
**Safety:** wear eye protection; the acid and alkali are irritants; cut agar on a tile with a sharp knife or scalpel carefully.
**Improving reliability:** repeat and calculate a mean; cut cubes accurately; stir; use the same timing end point (a white tile helps).
core.h: Practical idea: modelling diffusion with agar cubes
core.p: A common practical investigates the effect of size on diffusion. Cubes of agar jelly containing an indicator (for example phenolphthalein with dilute sodium hydroxide, which is pink) are placed in dilute hydrochloric acid. As the acid diffuses in, the pink colour disappears. Timing how long the cubes take to turn colourless shows the effect of SA:V. This is not one of the AQA required practicals, but it models the ideas and may be used as an exam context.

bullets: **Concentration gradient:** bigger difference = faster net diffusion (particles move down the gradient).
**Temperature:** higher temperature = particles have more kinetic energy and move faster = faster diffusion.
**Surface area:** bigger membrane area = more particles can cross at once = faster diffusion.
**Distance (diffusion path):** shorter distance = faster diffusion, linked to thin membranes.
When explaining, always say what the change **does to the particles** (more collisions or movement) and then to the **rate**.
core.h: Link to the rate of diffusion
core.p: SA:V is really a way of describing the surface area factor in diffusion. A bigger surface area lets more particles cross per second, but the amount that needs supplying depends on the volume. So what matters for supplying a whole cell or organism is the ratio. This links to the other two factors: a steeper concentration gradient and a higher temperature also speed diffusion, but neither can fix a very small SA:V in a big animal.

bullets: **Cold climate animals** (for example polar bear, Arctic fox): compact bodies with small ears give a **smaller SA:V**, so **less heat is lost**.
**Hot climate animals** (for example elephant, desert fox): large ears (big surface area) give a **larger SA:V**, so **more heat is lost** to help them cool.
**Small mammals** (such as shrews) lose heat quickly because of a large SA:V, so they must eat very frequently and have a high metabolic rate.
In an exam, **link the structure (SA:V) to the function (rate of heat loss)** and mention the environment.
This is an application of the same principle; you will not have been told the animal, so use the data and shape given.
core.h: Adaptations of large organisms that change their SA:V
core.p: Some animals have body shapes that change their SA:V to help with their lifestyle. A small SA:V reduces heat loss while a large SA:V increases heat loss, so animals in cold climates tend to be large and compact, while those in hot climates have larger extremities. This idea is often tested as an application question, so be ready to apply the same reasoning to heat transfer.

bullets: **Comparing ratios:** convert to the form X : 1 so you can compare easily (for example 24 : 8 = 3 : 1).
**Magnitude questions:** say how many times bigger one ratio is than another (for example 6 : 1 is **three times** greater than 2 : 1).
**Cuboids:** do not forget that opposite faces are equal; there are three pairs of faces.
**Scale factors:** if all lengths are multiplied by k, then areas are multiplied by **k²** and volumes by **k³**, so SA:V is divided by **k**.
Use appropriate **significant figures** and show your working; marks are given for method even if the arithmetic slips.
When interpreting a graph, describe the **trend** (decreases as size increases) and use data to support it.
core.h: Higher tier thinking and maths skills
core.p: Although the specification does not have separate Higher tier content here, Higher tier papers include harder calculation and reasoning about SA:V. You may need to work out the ratio for a cuboid or a sphere-like cell, compare two organisms, or explain an unfamiliar adaptation. Take care with units and clear step-by-step working. Express ratios in the form X : 1 when asked to compare.

exam: **1 mark** (State/Name): give the idea in a short phrase, for example 'a large surface area' or 'volume increases faster than surface area'.
**2 mark** (Explain/Give a reason): make a point and add the link, for example 'it has a small SA:V, so diffusion is too slow to reach inner cells'.
**Calculation marks:** show surface area (1), volume (1), ratio (1). Always write the ratio as X : 1 and include units for area and volume.
**Describe a trend** from a graph or table: say 'as the size increases, the SA:V decreases', then quote two data values with units.
**Explain why multicellular organisms need exchange surfaces and transport systems:** 'small SA:V', 'diffusion distance too great', 'inner cells too far from the surface'.
**Adaptations questions (3 to 4 marks):** for each adaptation write the feature + the effect: 'thin walls, so a short diffusion path; many capillaries, so a steep concentration gradient'.
**Command words:** 'Calculate' needs a number; 'Compare' needs similarities/differences with figures; 'Explain' needs reasons; 'Suggest' means apply your knowledge to an unfamiliar situation.
**6-mark extended answers:** structure around (1) SA:V definition and values, (2) the effect on diffusion, (3) examples of adaptations, (4) a conclusion.
**Use the key phrases:** 'relatively large surface area to volume ratio', 'sufficient transport of molecules into and out of the cell', 'short diffusion path', 'steep concentration gradient'.
**Practical questions:** state the independent, dependent and control variables, and explain why a result is reliable (repeats, mean) and valid (control variables).

mistakes.r: The surface area does increase, but volume increases faster, so the SA:V ratio gets SMALLER as organisms get bigger.
mistakes.w: Bigger organisms have a bigger SA:V because they have more surface.

mistakes.r: They have a large SA:V, which is why diffusion alone is enough for them.
mistakes.w: Single-celled organisms have a small SA:V so they are tiny.

mistakes.r: A cube has six faces: surface area = 6 × L². Volume = L³.
mistakes.w: Calculating surface area of a cube as L × 6 or L² only.

mistakes.r: SA:V means surface area first, then volume (SA ÷ V), usually written X : 1.
mistakes.w: Writing the ratio the wrong way round (volume : surface area).

mistakes.r: Surface area is in cm² and volume is in cm³; the final ratio has no units.
mistakes.w: Forgetting units, or writing cm instead of cm² and cm³.

mistakes.r: Diffusion is passive; it needs no energy from respiration. Active transport is the one that needs energy.
They can, but diffusion across the outer surface alone is too slow for inner cells, so they need exchange surfaces and a transport system.
mistakes.w: Large organisms cannot get oxygen at all by diffusion.

mistakes.r: Thin means a SHORT DIFFUSION PATH; large area is a separate feature. Name each feature and its effect.
mistakes.w: The exchange surface is thin so it is faster because it is smaller.

mistakes.r: Add the reason: volume increases faster than surface area as size increases.
mistakes.w: Just saying SA:V is smaller without explaining why.

summary: You must know that **substances move into and out of cells by diffusion** and that how well this works depends on the **surface area to volume ratio (SA:V)**. Single-celled organisms have a large SA:V so diffusion alone meets their needs; **multicellular organisms have a much smaller SA:V** so they need specialised **exchange surfaces** and a **transport system**. You also need to calculate and compare SA:V ratios (a maths skill that appears often in exams).

terms.d: The spreading out of the particles of any substance in solution, or particles of a gas, resulting in a net movement from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.
The total area of the outer surface of an object, measured in square units such as cm².
The amount of space inside an object, measured in cubic units such as cm³.
Surface area divided by volume; it compares the area available for exchange with the size of the organism or cell that must be supplied.
The difference in concentration between two regions; substances diffuse down a concentration gradient.
The distance particles have to travel to cross an exchange surface; a short path makes diffusion faster.
A specialised surface of an organism, adapted for the efficient transfer of substances, with a large surface area, thin membrane, good blood supply and (for gases) ventilation.
An organism made of just one cell, which has a relatively large surface area to volume ratio.
An organism made of many cells, which has a smaller surface area to volume ratio and needs exchange surfaces and a transport system.
A system such as the blood circulatory system (animals) or xylem and phloem (plants) that carries substances around an organism.
Moving air (or water) over a gas exchange surface to maintain a steep concentration gradient.
A process that does not need energy from respiration, such as diffusion.
Tiny air sacs in the lungs, with thin walls and a good blood supply, where gas exchange takes place.
Finger-like projections lining the small intestine that increase the surface area for absorption of digested food.
The number by which all lengths are multiplied when an object is enlarged; areas change by the square and volumes by the cube of this number.

worked.ans: 4 cm cube = 1.5 : 1; 2 cm cube = 3 : 1; the smaller cube has an SA:V ratio 2 times bigger.
worked.q: A student has a cube of side 4 cm and a cube of side 2 cm. Calculate the SA:V ratio of each cube and state how many times bigger the ratio is for the smaller cube. (4 marks)
steps: 4 cm cube: surface area = 6 × 4 × 4 = 96 cm². Volume = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 cm³.
2 cm cube: surface area = 6 × 2 × 2 = 24 cm². Volume = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cm³. SA:V = 24 ÷ 8 = 3, so 3 : 1.

worked.ans: Surface area = 22 cm²; volume = 6 cm³; SA:V = 3.7 : 1 (1 d.p.).
worked.q: A cuboid-shaped block of agar measures 3 cm × 2 cm × 1 cm. Calculate its surface area, volume and SA:V ratio. (3 marks)
steps: SA:V = 22 ÷ 6 = 3.67 (to 3 s.f.), which is 3.7 : 1 to 1 d.p.

worked.ans: The amoeba has a large surface area to volume ratio and a short diffusion distance, so diffusion across its surface supplies enough oxygen and food. The large animal has a smaller SA:V and many cells deep inside, so diffusion across the body surface alone is too slow. It therefore needs exchange surfaces and a circulatory system to transport substances to and from all its cells.
worked.q: Explain why a large multicellular animal needs a circulatory system but an amoeba does not. (4 marks)
steps: Link size to SA:V: the amoeba is small with a large SA:V; the animal is large with a small SA:V.
Link SA:V to diffusion distance: in the amoeba every part is close to the membrane; in the animal many cells are deep inside.
Link to consequence: diffusion alone is too slow for the animal to supply its inner cells, and its cells demand more oxygen.
Conclude: it needs exchange surfaces and a transport system (the blood) to carry oxygen and food to cells and remove waste.
